chapter_title: Secure Coding Patterns and Best Practices

screens.title: Secure Coding Patterns and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Proactive patterns to prevent reentrancy, DoS, and lifecycle errors

narration.text: In this chapter you'll move from spotting vulnerabilities to adopting concrete patterns that prevent them. We'll treat patterns as repeatable habits: validate inputs, update state, and isolate external calls. You'll learn the Checks-Effects-Interactions sequence as a default mental checklist, how pull-over-push payment designs avoid DoS and scale issues, and how pause controls and explicit state machines keep contracts in safe lifecycles. These are not academic rules — they are simple, practical techniques that reduce attack surface and make contracts auditable and maintainable. As we progress you'll see code examples that illustrate the vulnerable push approach and a safer pull approach, an emergency pause implementation using OpenZeppelin, and a state-machine pattern that prevents invalid transitions. You'll also leave with a checklist of best practices: keep logic small, rely on require and revert for early failure, use events for off-chain monitoring, and reuse battle-tested libraries. By the end you'll be equipped to refactor vulnerable code and design contracts that fail safely. Consider: which pattern will you mentally apply first when reviewing a function?

keyIdea.title: Core chapter promise
keyIdea.text: Adopt CEI, prefer pull payments, use emergency pause and explicit state machines to make contracts robust, auditable, and resistant to common attacks.

Why this matters

Small ordering mistakes or unchecked external calls can cost real funds. Applying a few patterns consistently prevents classes of bugs like reentrancy, DoS, and invalid state transitions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply a short checklist to any function that touches external code or Ether. First, you will consistently follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions order so reentrancy windows are eliminated. Second, you will design payments so recipients pull funds, avoiding large loops and many DoS scenarios. Third, you'll implement emergency stop controls to freeze critical operations when an incident occurs, giving you time to react. Finally, you will design and enforce state machines so functions only execute in appropriate lifecycle phases. Each objective pairs a concrete implementation skill with why it matters: CEI prevents reentrancy, pull payments improve scalability and safety, pause mechanisms give an operational kill-switch, and state machines reduce logical errors. As you practice these objectives, run small tests that validate transitions and withdrawals. These routines should become part of your code review checklist. Which objective will you prioritize adding to your next contract?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Practices
screens.subtitle: Concrete habits and tool choices to adopt

narration.text: Beyond patterns, this chapter expects you to adopt a set of engineering habits. Keep contracts small and composable so audits are tractable. Use require and revert to fail early; this reduces complex error paths. Favor proven libraries such as OpenZeppelin for access control and pause logic rather than reimplementing critical pieces. Emit events for all critical operations so off-chain tools and audits can reconstruct state changes reliably. Finally, write comprehensive tests: unit tests, integration tests, and use fuzzing where possible. Each habit shifts risk from runtime surprises to developer discipline and automated verification. For example, using OpenZeppelin's Pausable and Ownable reduces the chance of a buggy pause implementation. Writing a test to ensure withdraw functions only run in the success state catches lifecycle mistakes early. These practices are small upfront costs with high payoffs in safety and maintainability. screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) Pattern
screens.subtitle: A reliable ordering rule to prevent reentrancy and inconsistent state

narration.text: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is a simple, repeatable ordering for functions that interact with external contracts or send Ether. Define it as three steps: checks validate inputs and permissions using require or revert; effects update all contract state such as balances and status variables; interactions perform external calls or transfers. The core benefit is that state is always in a consistent, post-change form before any untrusted code can run. For example, when a withdraw occurs, ensure you set the user's balance to zero first, then perform the external transfer. A common misconception is that 'transfer' always prevents reentrancy; while transfer limits gas, it is not a substitute for CEI. Another pitfall is forgetting to update aggregated totals or flags before calling out, which leaves a reentrancy window. Practice: when you see a function that calls another contract, mentally run the CEI checklist. If any step is out of order, refactor. The takeaway is straightforward: ordering matters. Treat CEI as your default mental model whenever external calls exist. Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) Pattern means validate inputs, update storage, then interact externally so state cannot be manipulated during external execution.. In practical terms, a reliable ordering rule to prevent reentrancy and inconsistent state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CEI principle
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs, update storage, then interact externally so state cannot be manipulated during external execution.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › CEI Pattern
Definition
Checks → Effects → Interactions

Checks validate callers and preconditions. Effects update storage so the contract's invariants hold. Interactions call external code or transfer Ether only after state is final.

Example
// Pseudocode illustrating CEI
require(msg.value > 0);                 // Check
balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;     // Effect
(bool ok, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // Interaction
require(ok);
Common mistake

Updating storage after external calls leaves a time window for reentrancy. Do not rely on gas-limited transfers as the only defense.

Concrete checklist
  • Require checks for permission and bounds.
  • Perform all state writes and zero balances before calls.
  • Only then make external calls and handle failures.
Key Takeaway

Use CEI as a reflex. Ordering prevents most reentrancy problems and simplifies audits.

screens.title: Pull-over-Push Payments
screens.subtitle: Why recipients should withdraw their funds rather than receiving pushes

narration.text: Push payments attempt to send Ether to recipients in a single transaction, which sounds convenient but introduces two serious risks. First, looping over many recipients can exceed block gas limits and fail — a denial of service scenario. Second, if the push involves external calls, each transfer becomes an attack surface for reentrancy unless carefully guarded. The pull-over-push design avoids both by storing amounts in a mapping and letting each recipient call a withdraw function. This shifts gas costs to recipients and ensures each transfer operates under CEI ordering. The chapter provides a vulnerable push example that loops through participants and a secure pull example where payouts are recorded and withdrawn by recipients. A common misconception is that push is always faster or simpler; in practice, push creates brittle, non-scalable logic. When designing token distributions or rewards, prefer pull withdrawals or implement batch processing with startIndex and count so distribution can be split into safe chunks. The takeaway: design for scalability and safety by letting recipients claim funds on demand. Pull-over-Push Payments means let recipients withdraw allocated amounts to avoid gas and reentrancy issues inherent in large push loops.. In practical terms, why recipients should withdraw their funds rather than receiving pushes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pull beats push

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Pull vs Push
Vulnerable Push
// Vulnerable Push Payment
function distributeRewards() public onlyOwner {
    for (uint i = 0; i < participants.length; i++) {
        address recipient = participants[i];
        uint256 reward = rewards[recipient];
        if (reward > 0) {
            rewards[recipient] = 0; // State update
            (bool success, ) = recipient.call{value: reward}(""); // External call
            require(success, "Transfer failed");
        }
    }
}
Why it's risky

Loops across dynamic arrays can fail when the number of recipients grows. External calls inside loops also amplify reentrancy risk.

Secure Pull
// Secure Pull Payment
mapping(address => uint256) public payouts; // Amount available for withdrawal

function depositReward(address _recipient, uint256 _amount) public onlyOwner {
    payouts[_recipient] += _amount;
}

function withdrawReward() public {
    uint256 amount = payouts[msg.sender];
    require(amount > 0, "No pending rewards");

    payouts[msg.sender] = 0; // Effect: Clear balance FIRST
    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // Interaction: Send Ether
    require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
}
Key Takeaway

Store payouts and let users withdraw. This keeps operations atomic and scalable.

screens.title: Converting Push to Pull — Practical Steps
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach to refactor distributions safely

narration.text: When you identify a push-based distribution, convert it to pull in clear steps. First, stop trying to loop and transfer to many recipients in a single transaction. Instead add a mapping to record owed amounts per recipient. Second, provide a deposit or allocation function that increments the mapping for each recipient. Third, implement a withdraw function that follows CEI: verify the amount, zero the mapping entry, then transfer. Fourth, consider access controls so only authorized callers deposit allocations. Finally, prepare for edge cases: what if a recipient never withdraws? That leftover value remains in the contract until claimed, which is often acceptable and safer than failing all transfers. A common alternative is batch processing with startIndex and count to process distributions across multiple transactions; this is useful for owner-driven processing when recipients cannot be expected to claim. The essential idea is shifting gas and complexity to the claimant and enforcing CEI in each withdrawal. Ask yourself: which functions must be paused or guarded while refactoring? Converting Push to Pull — Practical Steps means replace loops with a mapping, add a withdraw function that follows cei, and optionally support batch processing for owner-driven work.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach to refactor distributions safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor steps
keyIdea.text: Replace loops with a mapping, add a withdraw function that follows CEI, and optionally support batch processing for owner-driven work.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Push → Pull Process
Step-by-step
  1. Add a mapping for owed amounts.
  2. Offer a deposit/allocation function to increase owed amounts.
  3. Implement withdraw with CEI: require, zero, call.
  4. Optionally add batch processing with controlled range to avoid gas limits.
Example decision

If recipients are active, pull payments are ideal. If recipients cannot act, provide a batched processing endpoint that processes a range of recipients per transaction.

Misconception

People think push is simpler because it centralizes payment. In reality it centralizes risk and gas cost, making the system brittle and prone to DoS.

Pro Tip

Record allocations immediately; never rely on iterating current arrays to compute owed amounts after the fact.

screens.title: Emergency Stop (Pausable) Mechanism
screens.subtitle: How and why to add an operational kill-switch

narration.text: An emergency stop or pause mechanism is a simple but powerful operational control. It lets an authorized role temporarily halt critical functions like deposits or withdrawals while an incident is investigated. The standard approach is a boolean paused state with modifiers such as whenNotPaused to guard sensitive functions. OpenZeppelin provides a Pausable contract that implements pause, unpause, and the whenNotPaused modifier; using it reduces the chance of a buggy home-grown pause. You should design pause so it only limits what you need: blocking deposits and transfers but not administrative diagnostic calls. A common misconception is that pause removes the need for other controls; it does not. Pause is a last-resort mitigation that buys time to fix bugs or upgrade contracts. Consider governance or multi-sig constraints on pause in production systems. When you add pause, add tests asserting functions revert in paused state and resume after unpause. The core idea: provide a controlled, reversible interruption to contain damage. Emergency Stop (Pausable) Mechanism means use pausable to halt critical operations during incidents, but keep pause narrow, reversible, and thoroughly tested.. In practical terms, how and why to add an operational kill-switch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pause as safety net
keyIdea.text: Use Pausable to halt critical operations during incidents, but keep pause narrow, reversible, and thoroughly tested.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Emergency Stop
Using OpenZeppelin's Pausable
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/security/Pausable.sol";

contract MyPausableContract is Ownable, Pausable {
    function deposit() public payable whenNotPaused {
        // ... deposit logic ...
    }

    function withdraw() public whenNotPaused {
        // ... withdraw logic ...
    }

    function emergencyPause() public onlyOwner {
        _pause();
    }

    function resumeOperations() public onlyOwner {
        _unpause();
    }
}
When to pause

Pause during active exploits or when a critical bug is discovered. Use it to stop state-changing operations while you patch or migrate.

Check

Test that functions revert with whenNotPaused and that only authorized roles can toggle pause.

screens.title: State Machine Design
screens.subtitle: Explicit states and guarded transitions prevent logic errors

narration.text: State machines make a contract's lifecycle explicit. Define an enum of valid states and require correct transitions with require statements or a reusable modifier. For example, a crowdfunding campaign might enumerate Setup, Funding, Success, Failed, Refundable, and Withdrawn. Only allow contribute while Funding, and only allow beneficiary withdraw when the state is Success. This prevents functions from executing at the wrong time and helps auditors reason about allowed behavior. A common error is implicit state determined by variables instead of a clear enum, which leads to subtle timing bugs. Another mistake is missing guards on state transition functions; always validate the current state before moving to the next. State machines also pair naturally with pause controls: paused should block operations independent of lifecycle state. When designing state transitions, write tests that try invalid transitions and assert they revert. The core benefit is clarity — both for the code and for future reviewers — and reduction of unintended execution paths. State Machine Design means use enums and modifiers to enforce where and when functions may run, preventing invalid operations and simplifying audits.. In practical terms, explicit states and guarded transitions prevent logic errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle clarity
keyIdea.text: Use enums and modifiers to enforce where and when functions may run, preventing invalid operations and simplifying audits.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › State Machine
Enum Example
enum State { Setup, Active, Paused, Completed }
State public currentState;

function activateContract() public onlyOwner {
    require(currentState == State.Setup, "Cannot activate from current state");
    currentState = State.Active;
}

modifier inState(State _state) {
    require(currentState == _state, "Invalid state");
    _;
}

function performActiveAction() public inState(State.Active) {
    // logic only executable in Active
}
Practical guidance

Map real-world lifecycle phases into enum values. Keep transitions strict and test every invalid path you can imagine.

Key Takeaway

Explicit states reduce ambiguity and eliminate calls at incorrect times, preventing logical vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Crowdfunding Starter — Review and TODOs
screens.subtitle: Understand the starter code and where to apply CEI, pull payments, pause, and state checks

narration.text: The hands-on activity provides a starter crowdfunding contract that already imports Ownable and Pausable and defines a CampaignState enum with Funding, Success, Failed, Refundable, and Withdrawn. The contract outlines storage for beneficiary, goal, deadline, totalRaised, contributions, and refundableAmounts. Your tasks are to implement contribute, withdrawFunds, claimRefund, and refine endCampaign so it does not iterate over contributors. When implementing contribute, validate funding state, the deadline, and msg. value, then update contributions and totalRaised as the effect. Do not perform any interactions in contribute. For withdrawFunds ensure you check the Success state, capture amountToWithdraw, zero totalRaised first, then transfer to beneficiary following CEI. For claimRefund require Failed state and make each contributor call withdraw their contribution: read amount, set contributions[msg. sender] to zero, then transfer. For endCampaign, set state based on totalRaised without attempting to loop through contributors; allow contributors to claim refunds later. Also ensure whenNotPaused guards deposit and withdrawal functions. These steps enforce CEI, enable pull refunds, and rely on the state machine to prevent invalid calls. Crowdfunding Starter — Review and TODOs means complete contribute, withdrawfunds, and claimrefund with cei and state checks; avoid iterating over contributors in endcampaign.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Crowdfunding Starter
Starter Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/security/Pausable.sol";

contract SecureCrowdfunding is Ownable, Pausable {
    enum CampaignState { Funding, Success, Failed, Refundable, Withdrawn }
    CampaignState public currentState;

    address public beneficiary;
    uint256 public goal;
    uint256 public deadline;
    uint256 public totalRaised;

    mapping(address => uint256) public contributions; // For individual contributions
    mapping(address => uint256) public refundableAmounts; // For pull refunds

    event Contribution(address indexed contributor, uint256 amount);
    event FundsWithdrawn(address indexed beneficiary, uint256 amount);
    event CampaignStateChanged(CampaignState newState);

    constructor(address _beneficiary, uint256 _goal, uint256 _duration) {
        require(_beneficiary != address(0), "Beneficiary cannot be zero address");
        require(_goal > 0, "Goal must be greater than zero");
        beneficiary = _beneficiary;
        goal = _goal;
        deadline = block.timestamp + _duration;
        currentState = CampaignState.Funding;
    }

    // Implement deposit function adhering to CEI and state machine
    function contribute() public payable whenNotPaused {
        require(currentState == CampaignState.Funding, "Campaign is not in funding state");
        require(block.timestamp < deadline, "Campaign has ended");
        require(msg.value > 0, "Contribution must be greater than zero");

        // Your CEI pattern here
        // Effect: Update state
        // Interaction: None for contribution, just state update
        // contributions[msg.sender] += msg.value;
        // totalRaised += msg.value;
        // emit Contribution(msg.sender, msg.value);
    }

    // ... additional functions omitted for brevity ...
Implementation notes
  • For contribute: effect only — update mappings and totals, emit event; do not call external addresses.
  • For withdrawFunds and claimRefund: zero balances first, then transfer and emit events.
  • For endCampaign: determine state using totals and deadlines; do not iterate over contributors.

screens.title: General Best Practices and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: A checklist to make your Solidity code robust and readable

narration.text: Beyond patterns, a set of engineering best practices dramatically improves contract safety. Keep contracts simple: smaller, focused contracts are easier to audit and reason about. Use require and revert aggressively to fail fast and document assumptions. When sending Ether, be deliberate: transfer and send come with a gas stipend but can cause DoS in modern environments; call is flexible but must be used with CEI and reentrancy guards. Handle external calls as if the callee is malicious — isolate them and do not permit them to change critical invariants. Emit events for off-chain monitoring and auditing; they provide an essential history for tools and auditors. Leverage established libraries like OpenZeppelin for access control, pausable behavior, and standard token implementations — this reduces the risk of introducing subtle bugs. Write comprehensive tests, including unit and integration tests and, where possible, fuzzing to exercise edge cases. Common mistakes include over-engineering, incomplete tests, and trusting external inputs without validation. The final practical tip: document assumptions clearly so reviewers can focus on security-critical decisions. General Best Practices and Common Mistakes means favor simplicity, fail early, treat external calls as untrusted, use events, reuse proven libraries, and test comprehensively.. In practical terms, a checklist to make your solidity code robust and readable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Favor simplicity, fail early, treat external calls as untrusted, use events, reuse proven libraries, and test comprehensively.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Best Practices
Simplicity & Composition

Split complex systems into smaller contracts and well-defined interfaces. Composability improves testability and auditability.

Fail early with require/revert

Validate inputs and state transitions at the top of functions so failures are obvious and localised.

Handle external calls as untrusted

Assume external contracts may be malicious and isolate their effects. Never let external code dictate internal invariants.

Events

Emit events for deposits, withdrawals, and state changes to aid monitoring and audits.

Libraries

Prefer OpenZeppelin for common patterns. Reuse reduces the chance of subtle security bugs.

Key Takeaway

Good engineering habits combined with secure patterns drastically reduce risk.

screens.title: Testing Secure Patterns
screens.subtitle: Unit tests, integration tests and the role of fuzzing

narration.text: Testing is the instrument that turns patterns into reliable practice. For CEI and pull payments, write unit tests that assert ordering and balances. For example, test that withdraw clears the recipient balance before the transfer and that a reentrant fallback cannot extract extra funds. For state machines, create tests that try invalid transitions and expect revert messages. Integration tests should simulate realistic flows: many contributors funding, deadline passage, endCampaign transitions, and both success and failure paths. The chapter emphasizes fuzzing as an advanced technique to exercise edge cases and unexpected inputs; fuzzing can reveal assumptions about bounds and ordering. A useful habit is to add tests that toggle pause and assert the guarded functions revert while diagnostic or admin functions remain available. Always include checks that events are emitted for off-chain monitoring. Testing reduces human error and makes upgrades safer. A common mistake is writing only happy-path tests; include negative tests and gas-limited scenarios to reveal DoS and edge-case failures. Testing Secure Patterns means write unit, integration, and negative tests, and use fuzzing to reveal edge-case assumptions in secure patterns.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Testing & Validation
Unit Tests

Assert CEI ordering, balance updates, and that withdraw sets balances to zero before transferring. Include negative tests that expect revert messages.

Integration Tests

Simulate campaign lifecycle, multiple contributors, deadlines passing, and success/failure transitions to validate the state machine and pause behavior.

Fuzzing

Use fuzzing to explore unexpected input combinations and edge cases that handwritten tests might miss, like extreme gas usage or unusual value distributions.

Key Takeaway

Tests are your safety net; aim for negative tests and lifecycle simulations, not just happy paths.

screens.title: Design Questions: Batch Transfers & Liquidation Guards
screens.subtitle: Applying patterns to token batches and lending liquidation

narration.text: Two assessment scenarios highlight how patterns guide design choices. First, a batchTransfer that loops over recipients and calls transfer for each is problematic because it risks running out of gas and becoming unusable — a denial of service risk. If transfer triggers hooks or external code, it also raises reentrancy concerns. A safer pattern is pull-over-push: allocate balances in a mapping and let each recipient call claimTokens to withdraw their allocation. Alternatively, implement batch processing with startIndex and count so the owner can process recipients in small gas-bound chunks. The second scenario involves a lending protocol's liquidateLoan function. To ensure it only runs on defaulted loans, model loan lifecycle with an enum and use a modifier or require check that enforces LoanState. Defaulted. For emergency halts across lending and borrowing, integrate a Pausable mechanism so borrow and repay use whenNotPaused. Both scenarios illustrate how CEI, state machines, and pause controls complement each other: CEI protects individual functions, state machines define valid times to act, and pause provides an operational break. The core lesson: combine patterns rather than rely on one alone.

keyIdea.title: Combine patterns
keyIdea.text: Use pull payments or batched processing for distributions, and use state checks plus pause for sensitive protocol operations like liquidation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Assessment Scenarios
Batch Transfer Problem

Looping transfers can hit gas limits and become unusable. Replace with pull withdrawals or process recipients in controlled batches.

Liquidation Guard
enum LoanState { Active, Defaulted, Liquidated, Repaid }
mapping(uint256 => LoanState) public loanStates;

modifier onlyDefaultedLoan(uint256 _loanId) {
    require(loanStates[_loanId] == LoanState.Defaulted, "Loan is not in default");
    _;
}

function liquidateLoan(uint256 _loanId) public onlyDefaultedLoan(_loanId) {
    // liquidation logic
}
Key Takeaway

Design choices must balance scalability, safety, and operational needs. Use combined patterns to address different risks.

screens.title: Common Mistakes — Think Like an Attacker
screens.subtitle: Typical oversights and how to avoid them

narration.text: The most reliable way to avoid mistakes is to adopt an adversarial mindset. Common oversights include over-engineering complex monolithic contracts, under-testing edge cases, trusting external inputs blindly, and leaving implicit state transitions. Over-engineering makes reasoning and auditing harder; instead, break functionality into narrow contracts with clear interfaces. Relying on external inputs without validation opens many attack avenues — always validate and assume the external contract may misbehave. Neglecting negative tests is another frequent error: happy-path tests are necessary but insufficient. Also, trying to perform large atomic operations over many participants without batching or pull mechanisms is a classic DoS trap. Finally, missing events or not emitting state-change events makes forensic analysis and off-chain tooling difficult. The remedy is a consistent review checklist: CEI ordering checks, pull-over-push for distributions, pause controls for emergencies, explicit state machines, use of OpenZeppelin, and full test coverage including negative and gas-bound scenarios. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Common Mistakes
Mistake: Implicit State

Avoid deriving lifecycle implicitly from variables. Use explicit enums and modifiers to guard functions.

Mistake: Large Atomic Loops

Loops that process many participants risk gas exhaustion. Prefer pull withdrawals or batched processing.

Mistake: Missing Tests

Only happy-path tests are insufficient. Add negative, lifecycle, and gas-bound tests.

Key Takeaway

Think like an attacker: challenge assumptions, write negative tests, and simplify designs to reduce risk.

screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the three most practical ideas to carry forward. First, the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern: always validate inputs, update state, then make external calls. This ordering greatly reduces reentrancy risks and systemic inconsistencies. Second, prefer pull-over-push payments for distributions: record owed amounts and let recipients withdraw, which avoids large loops and scales safely. Third, design clear state machines and add emergency pause controls. Explicit states prevent invalid calls and the pause mechanism gives you an operational stop-gap during incidents. These three concepts interact: CEI secures individual functions, pull payments address distribution scale, and state machines plus pause protect lifecycle and operations. Make them part of your code review checklist and your test suites. Which of these will you apply to your next contract first? screens.subtitle: Three more concise reminders from the chapter

narration.text: Here are three concise reminders to make these ideas actionable. First, use events everywhere you change important state so off-chain systems and auditors can reconstruct activity. Second, prefer established libraries like OpenZeppelin for critical patterns such as Ownable and Pausable instead of rolling your own. Third, invest in tests: unit tests, integration tests, and fuzzing will reveal assumptions and edge cases before deployment. These reminders complete the practical toolkit: patterns secure individual functions, libraries and events improve observability and correctness, and tests validate behavior. Make small changes now: add an event to a critical function, import Pausable into a contract, and write a negative test that tries an invalid state transition. Small steps compound into major safety improvements.
